prompt: In a reaction energy diagram, what does the horizontal axis, called the reaction coordinate, represent?

choices.text: The progress of the reaction from beginning to end
The total energy of all the reactants
choices.why: Energy is plotted on the vertical axis. The horizontal axis tracks how far the reaction has progressed.

choices.text: Time, measured in seconds
choices.why: The reaction coordinate shows the progress of the reaction from reactants to products, not a clock time; a fast and a slow reaction can share the same horizontal axis.

choices.text: The temperature of the reaction mixture
choices.why: Temperature isn't plotted on an energy diagram. The horizontal axis represents the progress of the reaction.

explanation: In an energy diagram, the vertical axis represents the total energy of all reactants, and the horizontal axis, called the reaction coordinate, represents the progress of the reaction from beginning to end (Figure 6.9.1).

prompt: As ethylene and HBr collide and the reaction begins, why does the energy level first rise?

choices.text: The electron clouds of the reactants repel each other
Heat must be added from outside before any reaction can start
choices.why: The rise comes from the reactants themselves: as they approach, their electron clouds repel each other.

choices.text: The new C−H bond forms, and forming a bond absorbs energy
choices.why: Bond formation releases energy. The rise comes from repulsion between the approaching electron clouds, before the C−H bond starts to form.

choices.text: The carbocation is already formed and is high in energy
choices.why: The carbocation forms only after the transition state is passed. The initial rise is due to repulsion between the reactants' electron clouds.

explanation: As the two reactants collide and reaction commences, their electron clouds repel each other, causing the energy level to rise. If the collision has enough force and proper orientation, the reactants continue to approach despite the rising repulsion until the new C−H bond starts to form.

prompt: What must a collision between ethylene and HBr have for the reactants to keep approaching until the new C−H bond starts to form?

choices.text: Enough force and the proper orientation
Enough force; orientation doesn't matter
choices.why: Force alone isn't enough. The section says the collision must occur with enough force and proper orientation.

choices.text: A negative ΔG° for the step
choices.why: The first step of this reaction has a positive ΔG°, yet it still occurs. What matters for each collision is its force and orientation.

choices.text: A catalyst to hold the molecules together
choices.why: No catalyst is involved here. Collisions with enough force and proper orientation carry the reactants over the barrier.

explanation: If the collision has occurred with enough force and proper orientation, the reactants continue to approach each other despite the rising repulsion until the new C−H bond starts to form, eventually reaching a structure of maximum energy, the transition state.

prompt: Which statement correctly describes a transition state?

choices.text: It is the highest-energy structure in a reaction step, and it is unstable and can't be isolated
It is a stable species that can be isolated partway through the reaction
choices.why: The transition state is unstable and can't be isolated; it sits at the energy maximum of the step.

choices.text: It is the lowest-energy point between reactants and products
choices.why: The transition state is at the top of the barrier, the structure of maximum energy, not at a minimum.

choices.text: It is the final product of the step
choices.why: From the transition state the reaction can go on to products or revert to reactants; it is neither one.

explanation: The transition state represents the highest-energy structure involved in a step of the reaction. It is unstable and can't be isolated, but it can be imagined as an activated complex of the reactants.

prompt: In the transition state for the first step of the reaction of ethylene with HBr (Figure 6.9.2), what is the state of the bonds?

choices.text: The C=C π bond and the H−Br bond are partially broken, and the new C−H bond is partially formed
The C=C π bond and the H−Br bond are fully broken, and the C−H bond has not begun to form
choices.why: In the transition state, bond breaking and bond making are happening at the same time; all three bonds are partial.

choices.text: The C−H bond is fully formed, and the C−Br bond is partially formed
choices.why: When the C−H bond is fully formed, the carbocation has been reached. The C−Br bond forms only in the second step.

choices.text: No bonds have changed yet; the molecules are just touching
choices.why: The transition state is an activated complex in which the old bonds are partly broken and the new C−H bond is partly formed.

explanation: The transition state can be imagined as an activated complex of the two reactants in which both the C=C π bond and the H−Br bond are partially broken and the new C−H bond is partially formed (Figure 6.9.2).

prompt: What is the activation energy, ΔG‡, of a reaction step?

choices.text: The energy difference between the reactants and the transition state
The energy difference between the reactants and the products
choices.why: That difference is ΔG°, the net energy change for the step.

choices.text: The energy difference between the transition state and the products
choices.why: That is the energy released when the transition state goes on to products. ΔG‡ is measured from the reactants up to the transition state.

choices.text: The total energy of the reactants
choices.why: ΔG‡ is a difference: how far above the reactants the transition state lies.

explanation: The energy difference between reactants and the transition state is called the activation energy, ΔG‡, and it determines how rapidly the reaction occurs at a given temperature. The double-dagger superscript always refers to the transition state.

prompt: In an energy diagram, which quantity determines the reaction rate, and which determines the position of the equilibrium?

choices.text: ΔG‡ determines the rate; ΔG° determines the position of the equilibrium
ΔG° determines the rate; ΔG‡ determines the position of the equilibrium
choices.why: That is backward. The barrier height (reactants to transition state) sets the rate; the difference between reactants and products sets the equilibrium.

choices.text: ΔG° determines both
choices.why: ΔG° says nothing about how high the barrier is, so it can't give the rate. Some exergonic reactions are slow (Figure 6.9.3b).

choices.text: ΔG‡ determines both
choices.why: ΔG‡ is measured to the transition state, not to the products, so it doesn't fix the equilibrium position.

explanation: The energy difference between reactants and the transition state, ΔG‡, defines the reaction rate. The energy difference between reactants and product, ΔG°, defines the position of the equilibrium (Figure 6.9.1).

prompt: Why does a reaction with a high activation energy proceed slowly?

choices.text: Few collisions occur with enough energy for the reactants to reach the transition state
The products are higher in energy than the reactants
choices.why: That describes a positive ΔG°, which concerns the equilibrium, not the rate. The rate depends on the barrier height.

choices.text: The reactants collide less often when the barrier is high
choices.why: The barrier doesn't change how often molecules collide; it changes how many of those collisions have enough energy to reach the transition state.

choices.text: The transition state is very stable, so the reaction stops there
choices.why: Transition states are unstable and can't be isolated. A high one is slow to reach, not slow to leave.

explanation: A high activation energy results in a slow reaction because few collisions occur with enough energy for the reactants to reach the transition state. A low activation energy results in a rapid reaction because almost all collisions occur with enough energy.

prompt: Reaction A has ΔG‡ = 60 kJ/mol and ΔG° = +10 kJ/mol. Reaction B has ΔG‡ = 100 kJ/mol and ΔG° = −50 kJ/mol. At the same temperature, which reaction is faster?

choices.text: Reaction A, because it has the lower activation energy
Reaction B, because it is exergonic
choices.why: Being exergonic (negative ΔG°) affects the equilibrium, not the rate. Exergonic reactions can be slow if their barrier is high (Figure 6.9.3b).

choices.text: Reaction B, because it releases more energy overall
choices.why: The energy released overall is ΔG°, which defines the position of equilibrium. The rate is set by ΔG‡, which is higher for B.

choices.text: They are equally fast, because ΔG‡ − ΔG° is 50 kJ/mol for both
choices.why: The rate depends on ΔG‡ alone, the energy difference between reactants and the transition state.

explanation: The activation energy ΔG‡ determines how rapidly a reaction occurs at a given temperature, and a lower ΔG‡ means a faster reaction. ΔG° defines the position of equilibrium and doesn't decide the rate, so reaction A (60 kJ/mol) is faster than reaction B (100 kJ/mol).

prompt: What is the approximate activation energy for the reaction of ethylene with HBr, in kJ/mol?
explanation: The reaction of ethylene with HBr has an activation energy of approximately 140 kJ/mol (34 kcal/mol), near the top of the 40 to 150 kJ/mol range typical of many organic reactions.

prompt: Reactions with activation energies below about what value, in kJ/mol, take place at or below room temperature?
explanation: Reactions with activation energies less than 80 kJ/mol take place at or below room temperature, while reactions with higher activation energies normally require a higher temperature to give the reactants enough energy to climb the activation barrier.

prompt: Which of these reactions would normally need a temperature above room temperature to proceed?

choices.text: One with ΔG‡ = 120 kJ/mol
One with ΔG‡ = 45 kJ/mol
choices.why: 45 kJ/mol is well under 80 kJ/mol, so this reaction takes place at or below room temperature.

choices.text: One with ΔG‡ = 70 kJ/mol
choices.why: 70 kJ/mol is still below the 80 kJ/mol cutoff, so this reaction can occur at room temperature.

choices.text: One with ΔG‡ = 60 kJ/mol and ΔG° = +30 kJ/mol
choices.why: A positive ΔG° doesn't decide whether heating is needed; the barrier does, and 60 kJ/mol is below 80 kJ/mol.

explanation: Reactions with activation energies less than 80 kJ/mol take place at or below room temperature, while reactions with higher activation energies normally require a higher temperature. Only the 120 kJ/mol reaction is above the cutoff.

prompt: As a rough generalization, in what range do the activation energies of many organic reactions fall?

choices.text: 40 to 150 kJ/mol
1 to 10 kJ/mol
choices.why: Barriers that small would be crossed by almost every collision. Many organic reactions have activation energies of 40 to 150 kJ/mol.

choices.text: 10 to 35 kJ/mol
choices.why: 10–35 is the same range expressed in kcal/mol, not kJ/mol. In kJ/mol it is 40 to 150.

choices.text: 500 to 1000 kJ/mol
choices.why: That is far too high; even the slow reaction of ethylene with HBr has a barrier of only about 140 kJ/mol.

explanation: As a rough generalization, many organic reactions have activation energies in the range 40 to 150 kJ/mol (10–35 kcal/mol). The reaction of ethylene with HBr, at about 140 kJ/mol, is near the top of that range.

prompt: Once the transition state for the first step of the ethylene–HBr reaction is reached, what can happen?

choices.text: It can either continue on to the carbocation or revert back to the reactants
It must continue on to the carbocation, because the barrier has been climbed
choices.why: Reaching the top doesn't commit the structure to products; it can also come apart and revert to reactants.

choices.text: It stays as a stable activated complex until more energy is added
choices.why: The transition state is unstable and can't be isolated. It goes on to products or back to reactants.

choices.text: It goes directly to bromoethane in a single step
choices.why: Bromoethane forms in the second step, after the carbocation reacts with Br^−. The first transition state leads to the carbocation.

explanation: Once the transition state is reached, the reaction can either continue on to give the carbocation product or revert back to reactants. When reversion occurs, the transition-state structure comes apart and free energy corresponding to −ΔG‡ is released.

prompt: A reaction step has ΔG‡ = 90 kJ/mol and ΔG° = +30 kJ/mol. How much energy, in kJ/mol, is released as the transition state goes on to the product?
explanation: When the reaction continues on from the transition state, the energy released corresponds to the difference between the transition state and the product. The transition state is 90 kJ/mol above the reactants and the product is 30 kJ/mol above them, so 90 − 30 = 60 kJ/mol is released.

prompt: Why is the first step of the reaction of ethylene with HBr described as endergonic?

choices.text: The carbocation is higher in energy than the starting alkene, so ΔG° is positive and the step absorbs energy
It has a large activation energy
choices.why: A large ΔG‡ makes a step slow, not endergonic. Endergonic means the product is higher in energy than the reactants (positive ΔG°).

choices.text: The carbocation is lower in energy than the starting alkene, so the step releases energy
choices.why: A step whose product is lower in energy would be exergonic. The carbocation lies above the reactants.

choices.text: Energy is released when the C−H bond forms
choices.why: Energy is released as the transition state goes on to the carbocation, but the carbocation still ends up above the reactants, so the net change is positive.

explanation: The net energy change for the step, ΔG°, is the difference in level between reactant and product. Since the carbocation is higher in energy than the starting alkene, the step is endergonic, has a positive value of ΔG°, and absorbs energy (Figure 6.9.1).

prompt: A reaction has a high ΔG‡ and a negative ΔG°. How is it classified in Figure 6.9.3?

choices.text: A slow exergonic reaction
A fast exergonic reaction
choices.why: A fast reaction has a low ΔG‡. With a high barrier, the reaction is slow even though it is exergonic.

choices.text: A slow endergonic reaction
choices.why: Endergonic means a positive ΔG°. A negative ΔG° makes the reaction exergonic.

choices.text: A fast endergonic reaction
choices.why: Both parts are reversed: a high ΔG‡ means slow, and a negative ΔG° means exergonic.

explanation: Speed depends on ΔG‡ and the sign of ΔG° tells whether a reaction is exergonic or endergonic. Figure 6.9.3(b) shows a slow exergonic reaction: high ΔG‡, negative ΔG°.
